title: cohort-buffer-profiling-and-latency-ladder-wip
content:
Summary
------
Working notes from exploratory tuning of a cohort-buffered continuous batcher and a new monitoring technique we're calling the "latency ladder" (progressive quantile tracking per cohort). Goal is to reduce p99/p999 tail without regressing throughput or increasing average cost. This doc is an experimental sketch + profiling outputs + next-step list.

Motivation / hypothesis
---------------------
- Continuous batching is great for unit cost, but multi-tenant arrival skew + heterogeneous request lengths creates tail spikes.
- We believe that isolating short/urgent requests into small & fast cohorts (cohort buffers) and tracking a latency ladder per cohort will allow targeted flush/prefill policies that reduce tail without trashing throughput.
- Secondary hypothesis: a lot of residual tail comes from non-application overheads (kernel wakeups, buffer copies, GC pauses in worker threads). Profiling should reveal which layer to attack.

Experiment design
-----------------
1) Implement a lightweight cohort-buffer layer on top of existing continuous-batcher: incoming requests are stamped with cohort tags (short/normal/long/interactive). Cohort buffer holds up to N_cohort requests or T_cohort ms before forwarding to coalescer.
2) Latency ladder: maintain per-cohort running quantiles at 5/25/50/75/95/99/99.9; expose via trace events so we can correlate cohort states with flush events.
3) Probe matrix: sweep N_cohort in {4,8,16,32}, T_cohort in {2,5,10,25,50}ms, and cohort assignment policy in {length-hint, token-estimate, random-weight}. Run each cell for 10m of steady-state traffic plus 2x short-burst phases.

Workload characteristics
------------------------
- Synthetic mix derived from production traces (anonymized): 60% short (<64 tokens), 30% medium (64-512 tokens), 10% long (>512 tokens).
- Arrival patterns: Poisson baseline with periodic microbursts (50-200 reqs/s for 1-3s) and a slow-changing diurnal shift for longer runs.
- Tokenization and KV-cache behavior matched by using the same model binary as prod (small model debug variant).

Metrics captured
---------------
- latencies: request start->first-byte, request start->completion, service queue time, batch formation time, kernel scheduling delay (from eBPF histograms)
- throughput: requests/s, tokens/s, GPU utilization (where applicable)
- economics: tokens-per-second per-GPU and inferred cost-per-token proxy
- fairness: per-tenant p99 / share-weighted slowdown
- ladder time series: per-cohort quantiles sampled every 500ms

Profiling approach
------------------
- Flamegraphs from 1s statistical profiles (perf) for critical worker threads during tail spikes.
- eBPF-based timestamps (bpftrace) to measure syscalls per-request, scheduler delay (time in TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE or TASK_RUNNING queues), and wakeup latency.
- GPU traces via nvprof / Nsight on integrated test cluster to check whether batching changes kernel launch patterns.
- Instrumented microtraces: insert short trace points around copy-in/copy-out, serializing (protobuf/JSON), and model-kv-cache lookup.

Representative run (run-id: ladder-2024-11-20-01)
--------------------------------------------------
Setup: N_cohort=8, T_cohort=5ms, cohort assignment=length-hint. 10m run (after warmup).
Baseline (no cohorts) from same trace: p50=36ms, p95=120ms, p99=340ms, p999=980ms.
Cohort-buffered: p50=38ms, p95=105ms, p99=210ms, p999=430ms. Throughput -1.8% (within noise). GPU utilization down 2% (because more small batches, but still above target).
Observations:
- p99 down ~38% relative to baseline, p999 down ~56%. Greatest wins for short/interactive cohort.
- Medium and long cohorts saw minimal change in median but a small reduction in p95.
- Tail spikes correlated with periods where cohort buffer fill time exceeded T_cohort and then multiple large batches were serialized onto the GPU, creating short windows of high kernel queueing.

Profiling highlights
-------------------
- Flamegraph top hotspot during a p999 event: significant time in copy routines (memcpy) and in kernel-space scheduler wakeup path (futex+epoll wake).
- eBPF histograms showed increased sched_delay_ms for a small subset of worker threads that were blocked on a lock during a flush path (lock contention on the batch-assembly mutex).
- NVProf traces showed frequent small kernels launched back-to-back, increasing overall kernel launch overhead; some latency came from asynchronous stream syncs.

Root-cause hypothesis
---------------------
1) Cohort flushes are creating bursty kernel-launch patterns that the current driver/stream configuration handles poorly: many small kernels increase per-request latency despite better batch composition.
2) Lock contention in the batch-assembly path during simultaneous cohort flushes amplifies scheduler delays (some threads get preempted while holding locks).
3) Copy patterns: we observed repeated memcpy of identical prefix tokens across batches; lack of cross-batch prefix caching in the host code is causing avoidable CPU work.

Mitigations tried (quick experiments)
-----------------------------------
- Staggered flush: add randomized jitter (0-2ms) to cohort flush deadlines => reduced synchronized kernel launches and lowered p999 by further ~10% on top of cohort-buffering.
- Per-flush semaphore rather than global mutex for assembly => reduced observed lock-hold times; p99 improved marginally.
- Host-side prefix dedupe cache (L1) for the most common short prefixes => CPU memcpy time reduced by 32% in microbench, translated to ~8% tail reduction.
- Batched kernel fusion experiment (coalesce tiny GPU kernels into a single combined kernel invocation) - prototype showed promise but requires runtime-level compatibility and a non-trivial change to our kernel launcher.

Tradeoffs / failure modes observed
----------------------------------
- Very small cohort sizes (N_cohort=4) reduced p99 for short requests but increased median latency for medium requests due to fewer coalesced tokens per GPU call; hurts unit economics.
- Increasing T_cohort to 25ms improves throughput efficiency (larger batches) but reintroduces tail spikes for urgent cohorts.
- Randomized jitter helps but does not totally eliminate back-to-back small-kernel bursts when multiple cohorts hit their deadlines coincidentally.

Open questions / next experiments
-------------------------------
- Can we make the scheduler aware of the GPU kernel queue depth and adapt flush jitter dynamically (feedback loop)?
- How well does per-cohort ladder tracking scale with 100+ cohorts (tenant scale)? Memory and metric cardinality concerns.
- Evaluate alternative fairness signals: instead of cohort-tag, use per-tenant urgency credits that decay; how does that interact with cohort buffers?
- Run longer (12–24h) runs with production replay to test rare edge cases (p9999 behavior).
- Work with driver team to profile kernel launch wall time and see if stream consolidation helps generally.

Action items (short-term)
-------------------------
- [ ] Run 4 full sweep cells for N_cohort {8,16} x T_cohort {5,10}ms with longer 30m steady-state runs (owner: Diego, ETA: 2024-12-06).
- [ ] Add per-thread lock hold time histograms to make contention reproducible (owner: Priya, ETA: 2024-11-28).
- [ ] Prototype a light-weight fused-launch shim (in Rust) to experiment with kernel fusion without changing main runtime (owner: Ethan, ETA: 2025-01-10).
- [ ] Add ladder cardinality stress test: simulate 200 cohorts and measure memory/metric cost (owner: Avery, ETA: 2024-12-15).

Notes to self / quick wins
-------------------------
- Prefix L1 cache is cheap and worth shipping as an opt-in flag.
- Jitter on cohort deadlines should be enabled by default but with a scheduling-aware backoff to avoid harming steady throughput.
- Documented the run id mapping in the experimental README (see linked_artifacts).

Appendix: Helpful command snippets
----------------------------------
- perf top sampling (on worker thread pid 12345): sudo perf record -F 99 -p 12345 -g -- sleep 10; sudo perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > perf-worker.svg
- bpftrace quick sched delay: sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:sched:sched_switch { @[comm] = hist(nsecs(ktime() - args->prev_time)); }'
- nvprof short trace: nvprof --profile-child-processes --print-gpu-trace --csv -f ./run_inference.sh

------------------

- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987
